title: The Last Words of the Edmund Fitzgerald
lines: November 10th, 1975. A ship longer than two football fields sails into a storm on Lake Superior. At 7:10 PM, her captain radios a calm message: We are holding our own. Minutes later, she was gone. All 29 men with her.
No mayday. No distress call. Just silence on the radio, and an empty spot on the radar.
So how does a ship that big disappear in minutes, on a lake? To find out, we go back one day.
November 9th. Superior, Wisconsin. The Edmund Fitzgerald leaves port with 26,000 tons of iron ore, bound for Detroit. Her captain, Ernest McSorley, has sailed these lakes for decades.
But a powerful November gale is sweeping toward the lake. Another freighter, the Arthur M. Anderson, sails a few miles behind her.
By the next afternoon, the storm hits. Winds near hurricane force. Waves more than twenty feet high crash over the deck.
Then the Fitzgerald reports trouble. A railing is down. Two vents are torn away. She's starting to lean. And both of her radars are dead.
Now she's sailing blind, through one of the worst storms in years. Her only eyes are the ship behind her.
The Anderson guides her by radio. At 7:10 PM, they ask how she's doing. The captain answers: We are holding our own.
Soon after, a snow squall clears. The Anderson's crew looks ahead. The Fitzgerald's lights are gone. And so is her blip on the radar.
Days later, the Navy finds the wreck, 530 feet down, broken in two. None of the 29 men were ever recovered.
But what sank her so fast that no one had time to call for help?

Investigators blamed leaky cargo hatches, slowly flooding the hold. Others believe she scraped a shallow shoal earlier that day. And some sailors describe three giant waves, striking one after another.
The truth is, no one knows for sure. Whatever happened, it happened so fast that the crew never sent a single call for help.
A year later, Gordon Lightfoot turned her story into a hit song. And every November 10th, a bell rings 29 times at Whitefish Point. Once for every man aboard.

notes: Real people died: respectful tone, no crew photos, no dramatised deaths.
